issues.description: req.stream → req.bounded_stream change is the real fix but is undocumented and unexplained
issues.detail: The substantive code change is one line in examples/things_advanced.py: req.stream.read() becomes req.bounded_stream.read(). This is the load-bearing change — bounded_stream respects Content-Length and prevents reads from blocking when the client lied about body size. But the PR description frames it as 'add req.content_length to req.stream.read()' which is wrong (no content_length arg was added in the example), and there's no comment explaining why bounded_stream matters. Data dominates: the bounded_stream wraps the raw stream with a Content-Length-bounded reader — that's the right data structure here, and it deserves one line of explanation.

issues.description: FAQ example is contrived and teaches the wrong thing
issues.detail: The new FAQ entry builds a PostTest resource whose only job is to demonstrate that you can override Content-Length in test headers. The mechanism being demonstrated (passing headers= to simulate_post) is one line; the surrounding 30+ lines of fixture, resource class, and branching status logic are scaffolding. A filter-shaped example would be: 'here is simulate_post with a custom Content-Length header; here is the assertion.' The resource class with nested if/else exists to make the test interesting, not to teach the actual API. Strip to the minimum that shows the header override.

issues.description: README.rst churn is mostly formatting, mixed with one semantic change
issues.detail: The README diff is dominated by black/ruff-style reformatting (trailing commas, line wrapping, %-format → .format, str concat → code_to_http_status). Buried in the noise is a real signature change: StorageError.handle(ex, req, resp, params) → handle(req, resp, ex, params). That's a behavioral fix worth calling out, but it's invisible in a 100-line formatting diff. Separate cosmetic churn from semantic changes — they review differently and bisect differently.

issues.description: Test assertions use parenthesized assert form
issues.detail: assert(result.status == falcon.HTTP_400) in the FAQ reads as a function call to assert. Python's assert is a statement; the parens suggest the author thought it was a function. Minor, but the FAQ is documentation — people will copy it. Write 'assert result.status == falcon.HTTP_400'.

issues.description: Trailing comma in single-element headers list is misleading
issues.detail: headers = [('Content-Length', '1'),] in the FAQ uses a list of tuples when the rest of the codebase (and the new tests in test_examples.py) use a dict. Two ways to specify headers in one PR's docs and tests is one too many — pick the dict form everywhere and the data shape is obvious.

issues.description: Two new test cases share setup but don't share a fixture
issues.detail: resp3 and resp4 in test_things_advanced both call testing.simulate_post with the same path and overlapping headers. The 'Authorization': 'custom-token', 'Content-Type': 'application/json' pair is repeated. Small enough that it doesn't matter today, but the function is now doing four unrelated assertions (GET 200, GET 200 again, POST 201, POST 400) in one body. Splitting into named tests would make failures more diagnosable. Not a blocker — n is small.

review.summary: SMALL-AND-COMPOSABLE for the test additions themselves — they're short, direct, and exercise the right two cases (happy POST, lying Content-Length). The real fix hides in a single line: req.stream → req.bounded_stream in examples/things_advanced.py, which swaps in the data structure that actually respects Content-Length. That's the Pike-shaped change and it deserves a one-line comment. The README diff is mostly cosmetic reformatting with one real signature change (handle parameter order) buried inside — separate those next time. The FAQ entry teaches the right API but wraps it in a contrived PostTest resource with branching status logic; strip it to the minimum that shows headers= overriding Content-Length. No P0 blockers — the bones are right, the framing around them is overbuilt.
